---
title: "What changed"
---

Newest first. Anything that moves a date or a deadline is also announced on ETL.

## 2026-09-17 — What each role holder prepares, week by week

Every role week in the [Weekly schedule](schedule.qmd) now opens with a **Roles this week** table: who holds each role, which method each Method Lead covers, which exemplar each Exemplar Analyst reads, and which exemplar each Skeptic attacks. Roles run in two tracks — Method Lead 1, Exemplar Analyst 1 and Skeptic 1 work one method and the paper that uses it; track 2 does the same for the other.

The Week 6 role walkthrough now uses this semester's actual Week 6 role holders instead of placeholder names.

## 2026-09-17 — Calendar reset: sixteen weeks, four Tuesday sessions, role roster published

**This replaces the 2026-09-10 plan below.** No session is asynchronous any more; every session meets in person.

**No class on 9/24 (추석).** Every session from the old Week 4 onward now runs one week later, and the final defense moves to **Week 16, Thursday 12/17** — the university's official make-up week. Week numbers on this site have changed accordingly: the problematization session is now Week 5 (10/1), Qualitative I is Week 6 (10/8), and so on through the defense in Week 16.

**Four sessions meet on a Tuesday** because the Thursday is unavailable: Week 8 (Tue 10/20), Week 10 (Tue 11/3), Week 11 (Tue 11/10), Week 13 (Tue 11/24).

Deadlines that moved as a result:

- Pre-proposal due: 10/15 → **Tue 10/20** (Week 8)
- Pre-proposal presentations: 10/22 → **10/29** (Week 9)
- Response-to-reviewers letters: 11/5 → **Tue 11/10** (Week 11)
- Horseshoe Wall graded checkpoint: 11/12 → **11/19** (Week 12)
- Final proposal due: 12/3 → **12/10** (Week 15)
- Final defense: 12/10 → **12/17** (Week 16)
- IRB protocol draft: 10/1 → **10/8** (start of Week 6)
- The Week 6 role walkthrough handout now runs on the 10/1–10/15 dates

**The role roster is published** in §4.1 of *How the course works*, with names as initials. The class has twelve students, so the numbers there were corrected: five or six turns each, and five entry tickets per week rather than nine.

## 2026-09-10 — Three more sessions cannot meet; make-ups set

Three conference dates collide with the seminar, on top of the Chuseok block already flagged for Week 4:

- **Week 8 (10/22)** — 건축학회 학술발표대회
- **Week 10 (11/5)** — 건설관리학회 학술발표대회
- **Week 13 (11/26)** — AKC 2026

All four blocked sessions are made up. **Weeks 4, 10 and 13 run asynchronously with the role rotation intact** — if your turn falls in one of them you write the deliverable instead of presenting it, and it still counts as your turn. **Week 8 needs a live session**, because it is the pre-proposal presentations and peer review; the make-up date is being fixed and will be announced on ETL.

The response-to-reviewers letters, currently due in Week 10, respond to peer review from Week 8. That deadline follows the Week 8 make-up date and will be announced on ETL rather than moved quietly here.

Shifting the whole calendar back a week — listed as an option while Chuseok was the only conflict — is no longer viable. Four blocked Thursdays would push Week 15 past 12/10 into the exam period.

## 2026-09-04 — Week 2 required reading changed

The one reading to do if you do nothing else for Week 2 is now Halpin, D. W. (2007). "Fifty years of progress in construction engineering research." *JCEM*, 133(9), 635–639. It has been added to the Week 2 list.

Levitt (2007) stays on the list — it is still the forward-looking companion to Halpin's retrospective — but it is no longer the priority pick. If you already read Levitt after Week 1, nothing is wasted; read Halpin as well.

## 2026-09-02 — Week 2 preparation

Week 1 now ends with three things handed to you rather than none: your era team for the Week 2 workshop (drawn at random), the landmark works your team presents, and the JCEM volume you code in the Week 2 lab. Read them before Week 2 — the workshop is a prepared presentation, not an in-class reading session.

The landmark works are now named on the schedule with full citations — two per era, and three for 1955–75, where Gates (1967) and Carr (1982) are read against each other as a matched pair. All nine are journal papers.

## 2026-09-02 — Initial publication

First version of the course site. Replaces the PDF syllabus circulated previously.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How to read this page

Entries record substantive changes only — new readings, moved deadlines, restructured weeks. Typo fixes and formatting are not logged. If you need the exact state of the syllabus on a given date, the full commit history is on GitHub.
:::
